records.current_summary:
A gubernatorial executive order (August 30, 2023) narrows the legal definitions of 'male' and 'female', declares a person's biological sex fixed at birth, ends state recognition of transgender people, and backs single-sex spaces for bathrooms and changing rooms - mostly resident-facing, but it signals an administration willing to use state machinery against gender identity.

Below the national score 0.36.

prison_adds.title: Transgender rights in the United States — Wikipedia (federal prison-placement rule + August 2022 Nebraska ruling)
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia: under the January 2017 Obama-era Bureau of Prisons guidelines trans prisoners could be transferred to facilities of the gender they identify with, but on May 11 2018 the BOP rescinded the guidelines so that assigned sex at birth once again determines where trans prisoners are jailed; it then documents the Nebraska-specific case: in August 2022 a federal judge in Nebraska ruled against a transgender woman who had been denied gender-affirming care in prison and placed in a cell with a male sex offender who sexually assaulted her, holding there was insufficient evidence of deliberate indifference to her gender dysphoria and that she had not proven more than minimal injuries from the assault, finding no support that a substantial risk could be inferred from a prospective cellmate's sexual-offence conviction 'coupled with the alleged vulnerability of a transgender inmate transitioning to a woman in a men's prison'. Confirms Nebraska practices birth-sex (men's prison) placement and that the placement followed her there.

prison_adds.title: Transgender inmate loses lawsuit over prison's treatment for her gender dysphoria — Lori Pilger, Lincoln Journal Star (via Norfolk Daily News, archived)
prison_adds.summary: Lincoln Journal Star (Lori Pilger, Aug 10 2022, updated Aug 11 2022; archived by the Wayback Machine after the original page went dead): U.S. District Judge Brian C. Buescher ruled for Nebraska prison officials and workers sued by a transgender inmate identified only as 'Jane Doe', who was diagnosed with gender dysphoria and transitioning to be a woman while held in Nebraska's men's prison. The judge dismissed her claims of failure to treat her dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery, and failure to protect her: he previously dismissed the claim that guards failed to protect her after she was placed in a cell with a convicted sex offender who victimized her, wrote that 'without medical evidence, no reasonable jury could conclude that the providers were deliberately indifferent to Doe's serious medical need', and said she had not plausibly alleged more than de minimis injuries from the assault. Primary news documentation that Nebraska housed her by assigned birth sex among male prisoners and celled her with a male sex offender.

records.current_summary:
South Carolina's facility ban, enacted 2024, was expanded in 2026 to colleges and universities when the governor signed House Bill 4756 on May 15, 2026, requiring students in public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching sex assigned at birth.

The July 2026 assessment counts the expansion, raising the state's tier to 'Worst Laws Passed'; South Carolina is part of the 18-state birth-sex-definition group and scores below the national score 0.36.

prison_adds.title: Missouri Ends Gender-Affirming Care for Transgender Inmates - Metro Weekly
prison_adds.summary: Metro Weekly (11 Jul 2026), reporting on Missouri's law banning gender-affirming care for transgender inmates, records that per the Transitics tracker South Carolina is one of four states (with Tennessee, Arkansas and Utah) holding 'freeze-frame' policies that restrict the treatments transgender inmates may receive while incarcerated. This is the only South Carolina trans-prisoner-specific policy finding surfaced in the mandated search window; it documents an in-prison treatment restriction, not a housing-placement rule, and the article records no South Carolina case or ruling on cell placement, special units, or solitary/segregation for trans prisoners.

records.current_summary:
Tennessee is the only state in the country with a standing criminal ban on gender-expressive performance: the Adult Entertainment Act (2023) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment' — defined to include 'male or female impersonators' — anywhere a child could see it, at up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine for a first offence and a 1–6 year felony on repeat. The ban is enforceable and current: the appeals court revived it on standing grounds and the Supreme Court declined review (February 2025), so a visitor presenting in drag faces live charging exposure today rather than a dead-letter law.

For practical safety, killings of trans women run at 7.8 per 100k per year — above the general national homicide rate.

prison_adds.title: Transgender rights in Tennessee (Wikipedia) — Prison section
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia state-rights article, Prison section (accessed 4 Oct 2026): in April 2024 the Tennessee State Legislature passed a bill banning gender-affirming care for Tennessee inmates; and under the 2026 'Riley Gaines Women's Safety and Protection Act' transgender inmates are to be placed in prisons based on their sex assigned at birth (birth-sex placement mandate). The same 2026 Act also bans trans women from women's shelters (adjacent provision).

records.current_summary:
Texas operates one of the country's most actively enforced anti-trans regimes. Its facilities law (the SB 8 'Women's Privacy Act', in force 4 December 2025) produced enforcement within days: state troopers checked identification at women's restrooms in the Capitol while cities and campuses adopted sharply divergent compliance and evasion policies, and the attorney general opened the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry of its kind — against an Austin school district, escalated with a second records demand in April 2026 after a tip-line complaint.

Violence exposure is the national worst in absolute terms: 44 recorded killings of trans women over 2008–2025 (about 7.6 per 100k trans women per year; the monitoring project frames all rates as undercount floors). A July 2026 law-by-law legal-risk assessment grades Texas in its top 'Do Not Travel' tier.

prison_adds.title: Transgender rights in Texas (Wikipedia)
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia state-rights article (accessed 4 Oct 2026): Governor Abbott signed the Women's Privacy Act on 22 September 2025; it requires bathrooms matching the sex on one's birth certificate and explicitly applies to public schools, universities, prisons and Texas government buildings, with $25,000 (first) / $125,000 (subsequent) facility fines, effective 4 December 2025. Documents that Texas' most recent gender-placements statute reaches prisons — but on restroom use, not on cell/facility assignment or trans-prisoner housing placement.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ people in prison (Wikipedia) — Gibson v. Collier (2019) ruling
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia article on LGBTQ prisoners (accessed 4 Oct 2026), Gibson v. Collier section: Vanessa Lynn Gibson, a transgender woman incarcerated in Texas by the Texas Department of Criminal Justice and diagnosed with gender dysphoria, was denied gender-confirmation surgery because TDCJ's official treatment policy excluded GCS. The federal district court denied the state's immunity defences but ruled against her on the Eighth Amendment claim; the Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal (no deliberate indifference; refusing GCS is a permissible medical choice under Kosilek), with Judge Barksdale dissenting on summary-judgement procedure.

records.current_summary:
Afghanistan under the Taliban — the nation's current ruling movement — is the most hostile environment on this map for a transgender person. A 2024 Morality Law obliges the regime's virtue police to prevent "homosexuality" and "lesbianism", including "even if with one's own spouse"; the ruling movement applies the death penalty for same-sex relations under its interpretation of Sharia; and documented practice against LGBTIQ people includes beatings, sexual violence in detention, forced confessions, and house-to-house searches. Transgender residents report living in hiding, in windowless rooms, for years.

There is no legal recognition, no protection, no functioning consular protection, and no tourism infrastructure that would allow a visitor to blend in. A discovered trans visitor would face the same enforcement apparatus as local LGBTIQ people: detention with routine sexual and physical abuse of queer detainees, prosecution for moral crimes, and corporal punishment that international experts say is escalating into 2026.

This is the reference point for the very bottom of the risk scale.

prison_adds.title: Even If You Go to the Skies, We'll Find You: LGBT People in Afghanistan After the Taliban Takeover (Human Rights Watch / OutRight Action International)
prison_adds.summary: HRW/OutRight 43-page report (26 Jan 2022, 60 interviews) documents that since the Taliban takeover of 15 Aug 2021, LGBT Afghans have faced threats, assault, blackmail and wrongful-detention risk, with Taliban members using leaked personal data to pursue individuals considered gay or gender-nonconforming. Thin for the prison-housing axis: the report documents detention-related dangers for LGBT Afghans but contains no placement practice for trans prisoners - no birth-sex-vs-identity housing rule, no trans special units, and no solitary/segregation practice is described; it recommends the Taliban end discrimination and violence against LGBT people.

records.current_summary: Angola demands real caution from trans visitors. The 2020 Penal Code decriminalised same-sex conduct AND prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation — one of Africa's stronger statutory packages on paper. A 2024 shadow report by Angolan LGBT organisations (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, Movimento T and others) documents the gap: discrimination persists across health, education and employment; trans people have no legal gender recognition; and violence goes under-investigated. Luanda has a visible, organised community.

prison_adds.title: Human Rights Violations Against LGBTQI+ People in Angola — Shadow Report 2024 (Angolan CSOs; African Commission 81st session)
prison_adds.summary: Thin: the 2024 Angolan CSO shadow report (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, Movimento T, ASTA and others) contains no data on where trans prisoners are housed in Angola — nothing on birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, or solitary/segregation practice. Closest documented finding: in June 2024 a transgender woman in Viana (Luanda) was attacked by police officers because of her gender identity, suffered physical injuries, was arbitrarily detained by Esquadra 43 and subjected to degrading treatment, with the case under investigation by the judicial military police of the Provincial Command of Luanda (police custody; no prison placement information). It also notes the 2020 Penal Code criminalises discrimination based on sexual orientation with up to two years' imprisonment.

records.current_summary: Antigua and Barbuda demands real caution. The High Court struck down the buggery/gross-indecency laws in July 2022, reading the constitutional bar on sex discrimination to cover sexual orientation and gender identity. No LGR, no anti-discrimination statute, and residual social hostility; tourist resort areas are insulated.

prison_adds.title: Antigua and Barbuda | Outright International
prison_adds.summary: Thin: Outright International country profile (page states 'Last Update: March 12, 2026'; fetched and subject-verified). The Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court's 2022 ruling struck down Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995, and read the constitutional bar on sex discrimination as inclusive of sexual orientation and gender identity; there are still no explicit anti-discrimination protections, same-sex unions are unrecognised, and transgender people are particularly vulnerable because no legal gender recognition mechanism exists. The profile contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement (birth-sex vs identity placement), special units, or solitary/segregation practice for Antigua and Barbuda.

records.current_summary:
Australia is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court’s landmark Tickle v Giggle ruling confirmed that gender-identity discrimination protection covers trans women as women — with compensation awarded. States have modernised rapidly: Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections (April 2024) and NSW, another state, passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction; and marriage equality has held since 2017 (relevant to same-sex partners travelling together).

Counterweights: the Tickle case itself arose from organised exclusionary activism, which is vocal in Australia; ANROWS research documents systemic discrimination and harassment of trans people; and a NSW court granted a trans woman an apprehended-violence order against a Binary Australia activist who had targeted her — real harassment, but also functioning legal recourse.

For a visitor: full legal protection and functioning courts; low incident probability; border and document-screening practice is not detailed in the current sources.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ people in prison (Wikipedia; Australia section)
prison_adds.summary: Queensland placement policy: the 2009 Corrective Services procedure on transgender prisoners was assessed as largely ineffective (Jenny Samiec, Queensland Law Student Review 2009). Replacement oversight came via the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022 (fully in force 2023), whose August 2023 inspection standards for Queensland prisons and youth detention centres direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally to be admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender. Staff still hold discretion at admission, and only transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that process - so Queensland placement is identity-based with a discretionary admission caveat and a surgery exception.

records.current_summary: Belize demands real caution. The Court of Appeal struck down the sodomy law in 2016 (Orozco v AG) — the Caribbean's first decriminalisation ruling; Belize has an organised community (UNIBAM) and anti-discrimination employment protection. No LGR; gang violence in Belize City is a general risk.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ people in prison - Wikipedia
prison_adds.summary: Thin for Belize: the article (fetched, HTTP 200) surveys how LGBTQ prisoners worldwide are affected by strip-searching, solitary confinement, a disproportionate-incarceration risk, and transgender placement debates (including the US context), but its only Belize mention is a 'Violence in Belize' navbox taxonomy link. It contains no Belize-specific practice: no birth-sex-vs-identity housing rule, no trans special units, and no solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners in Belize; no usable placement finding.

records.current_summary:
Brazil combines some of the world's strongest legal protections for transgender people with a high level of real-world violence — the classic gap between law and practice. Courts allow name and gender-marker changes without surgery, the Supreme Court has criminalised transphobia (making it punishable like racism), courts fine businesses that discriminate, and official guidance affirms trans people's right to use bathrooms matching their identity.

For visitors, big-city queer life is vibrant and highly visible — São Paulo hosts the world's largest Pride parade — and the law is unambiguously on a trans traveller's side. The practical risks are concentrated in nightlife and app-based meetings: a majority of physical violence against LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo happens at night, and robbery schemes luring gay men via dating apps have been fatal.

Exercise particular caution after dark, with nightlife and app meetings, and in peripheral areas. Violence against local trans people (Brazil records the world's highest absolute toll) is heavily concentrated in poor and marginalised communities, not tourist areas.

prison_adds.title: Resolução CNJ n. 348 de 13/10/2020 (alterada pela Resolução n. 366/2021) — diretrizes para o tratamento da população LGBTI custodiada ou privada de liberdade (Conselho Nacional de Justiça)
prison_adds.summary: Brazil's National Council of Justice (CNJ) Resolution 348 of 13 Oct 2020, as amended by Resolution 366 of 20 Jan 2021, is the national framework for where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed: a person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing (Art. 4º); on arrest, the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person is consulted about their preference (Art. 7º), and the judge must inform them of the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it general population or specific wings/cells (Art. 8º); the declared preference is recorded and a later change of placement is possible, with transfers prioritised in cases of violence or serious threat (Art. 9º). LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited (Art. 11, VI–VII). The resolution entered into force after publication (120 days, extended to 180 days by Res. 366/2021).

prison_adds.title: Elas também não são mulheres?: Travestis e mulheres transexuais em situação de prisão no Rio de Janeiro (Dilemas — Revista de Estudos de Conflito e Controle Social 17(2), 2024, e60615)
prison_adds.summary: Peer-reviewed census study (Alves-da-Silva & Bonan, Dilemas 17(2), 2024; lead author also of the LGBTI health division of the Rio de Janeiro state penitentiary administration, SEAP-RJ) of travestis and transgender women in prison in Rio de Janeiro state: 138 self-declared travesti/trans-woman inmates were interviewed inside eleven units deemed 'masculine' in the metropolitan region (April–June 2021, via the SEAP's SIPEN database). It documents that in the Rio state system travestis and trans women are housed in units treated as masculine, with some held in so-called 'neutral' or 'security' units, and frames male-unit placement as a double punishment combined with recurring basic-rights violations; it also cites the 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting them parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units (hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics) and national norms (2014; 2020) that let them be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

records.current_summary:
Canada is exceptionally safe for trans visitors — the strongest of the large Western countries. Gender identity and expression are protected grounds in the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code’s hate-crime provisions (Bill C-16, 2017); most provinces offer self-declaration legal gender recognition; federal documents offer an X marker; and healthcare coverage is universal. There are no bathroom laws, no border friction (Canadian authorities have not issued or received trans-traveller warnings), and courts consistently enforce protections.

The counterweights are real but climate-level: police-reported hate crimes have risen six consecutive years (+169% since 2018), with gender identity/expression crimes among the fastest-growing categories; Egale documents a rising organised anti-trans movement; and Alberta/Saskatchewan have enacted resident-facing policy rollbacks (school pronoun and healthcare restrictions). A 2022 federal survey found 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ respondents experienced identity-based violence in five years — 90% of it verbal abuse, 17% physical.

For a visitor: full legal protection, functioning recourse, low probability of anything beyond verbal harassment in hostile pockets; the current sources report no marriage or partner-travel friction.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ people in prison — Canada section (Wikipedia)
prison_adds.summary: Placement policy: after Bill C-16 (2017) banned discrimination based on gender identity, transgender prisoners were to be placed in correctional facilities based on their gender identity, and Prime Minister Trudeau promised to review transgender prison assignment to ensure facilities match gender identity; transgender prisoners imprisoned for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. A 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security but with some concerns about risk to other prisoners; a 2022 CTV report alleged gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault. No special-unit or solitary/segregation policy detail beyond the federal identity-based placement rule.

prison_adds.title: Barbara findlay (Wikipedia) — Synthia Kavanagh case
prison_adds.summary: Documented case: the article records that Canadian lawyer Barbara findlay represented Synthia Kavanagh, a transgender prisoner, in litigation concerning gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's correctional institution — evidence that Canadian trans-prisoner placement and gender-affirming care were litigated in court. The Wikipedia article gives no dates or final outcome for the case, so this add is thin on specifics.

records.current_summary:
Switzerland is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition has worked by self-declaration since January 2022 — a personal declaration before the civil registrar, with no court or medical requirements (binary male/female only; no non-binary marker). Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2022 (approved by referendum), gender-neutral rape law took effect in 2024, and employers have a legal duty of care toward trans employees. General crime is exceptionally low.

The notable legislative shortcoming — flagged by the ILGA Rainbow Map and by the government's own review — is that the criminal hate-crime and hate-speech provision (Article 261bis) covers sexual orientation but not gender identity. So a person targeted specifically for being trans does not benefit from that aggravation in criminal law, though the protections available through employment and constitutional law are broader. Reported hate crimes against LGBTIQ people have risen about fivefold since 2020 (around six per week, but from a low absolute base of ~309 cases in 2024).

The federal government adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against LGBTIQ hate crime in January 2026 (running to 2030), signalling a pro-trans institutional direction. There is no rollback movement.

prison_adds.title: Gesetz über den Justizvollzug (Justizvollzugsgesetz, JVG) vom 13. November 2019 — Basel-Stadt detention law (TGNS)
prison_adds.summary: Primary legal text of the canton of Basel-Stadt's detention law (JVG, adopted 13 Nov 2019 by the Grand Council). §2 Trennungsvorschriften requires separation of female and male detainees and stipulates that 'the gender identity of the detained person is respected as far as possible' (Die Geschlechtsidentität der eingewiesenen Person wird soweit möglich beachtet); the prison directorate may deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority. This is the explicit 2019 inclusion of gender identity in a Swiss detention law aimed at protecting transgender people's placement in correctional facilities.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Switzerland — placement of transgender people in correctional facilities (Wikipedia)
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia overview of Swiss LGBTQ rights records that in November 2019 the Grand Council of Basel-Stadt voted to include 'gender identity' in its law on detention to better protect transgender people in regard to placement in correctional facilities, citing the TGNS-documented JVG. No national (federal) trans-prisoner placement rule is documented in the article — placement practice is cantonal; no Swiss case law, special trans units or federal solitary-confinement practice for trans prisoners are noted.

records.current_summary:
Côte d'Ivoire is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp recent deterioration. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised, but in late 2024 the country saw a wave of violence: social-media influencers exhorted followers to 'hunt' gay and gender-nonconforming people, and dozens of assaults and beatings followed. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and police response to the hunt wave was inadequate.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but the 2024 hunt-down campaign makes visible gender nonconformity dangerous, especially in the largest city (Abidjan).

prison_adds.title: Côte d'Ivoire | Country Page — Human Rights Watch
prison_adds.summary: Thin: no usable prison-housing finding. HRW's Côte d'Ivoire country page contains no document, case or report on transgender prisoners: 'LGBT Rights' appears only as a topic-facet link, and no HRW publication is listed on where trans detainees are housed (birth-sex vs identity placement), special units, or solitary/segregation practice in Ivorian prisons.

records.current_summary:
Costa Rica is workable for trans visitors — Central America's strongest jurisdiction by a wide margin. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971; marriage equality arrived in 2020 via the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion 24/2017 (which also established the right to legal gender recognition across the region); and trans people can change their name and photo on ID documents administratively. Institutions function: an ombudsman, a constitutional chamber (Sala IV) with a long pro-equality record, and universal healthcare that covers transition-related care.

Counterweights are modest: the Catholic Church is the official religion and culturally influential; the ID process changes name and photo but not the sex marker itself; and anti-discrimination enforcement is uneven. There is no bathroom debate of consequence, no police targeting, and tourist infrastructure is accustomed to diverse visitors. San José has a visible scene.

prison_adds.title: Transexuales reclusos en carceles nacionales podran optar entre prision de hombres o mujeres (AmeliaRueda.com)
prison_adds.summary: AmeliaRueda.com (Alonso Mata Blanco, 25 Jun 2017): Costa Rica's Justice Ministry (Vice-Minister Marco Feoli) announced that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual may choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility - relocation to the facility matching gender identity, strictly voluntary, decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists; a circular ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners, an exclusive module for trans people was under consideration, and Spain's system was cited as the model (protocols for vulnerable prison populations developed with CEJIL since 2016). Official policy-level documentation of placement-by-gender-identity in the regional context.

prison_adds.title: Stephanie, la transgenero que vive en la carcel rodeada de hombres | CR Hoy
prison_adds.summary: CRHoy (Javier Paniagua, 22 Jun 2019): Stephanie, a trans woman serving ~6 years for drug-trafficking complicity, is held at CAI Orosi de Cartago - a men's facility ('en esa sede solo hay hombres'); she transitioned while incarcerated and says prison offers 'solo hay dos opciones: o sos hombre o mujer aqui'. The Justice Ministry told CRHoy there were 23 transgender people in the national system at the time. Stephanie recounts identity-targeted abuse including a broomstick-handle rape at La Reforma (Alajuela) witnessed by a custodian. Shows that despite the 2017 choice policy, trans women were still found in men's facilities in 2019 and faced violence with custodial inaction.

records.current_summary:
Ecuador is a country that demands real caution from trans visitors. Legal gender recognition has existed since 2016, and the legal framework is now among the region's strongest. The 2024 reform lets adults change name and sex/gender on the identity document directly through the civil registry (one time, no surgery), and in 2024-25 court rulings extended document changes to trans adolescents and reprimanded the legislature for stalling trans-rights implementation.

The violence side is severe: a monitoring group documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023 with inadequate state response, and the "internal armed conflict" against gangs has intensified general violence since January 2024, with two more LGBTQ people killed in its first weeks; Quito and Guayaquil, the two main cities, carry real street risk, and police capacity is consumed by the security crisis.

For a visitor: documents and expression are legally protected, but the probability of encountering violence if outed in public is among the highest in the region right now.

prison_adds.title: Trans Women in Ecuador's Prisons | PrisioTrans Human Rights Program
prison_adds.summary: Silueta X (leading Ecuadorian trans-rights organisation), PrisioTrans program, documents 2011-2026: trans women in Ecuador's almost universally male prisons are held in male spaces and face gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and health-care barriers. Key cases: trans woman Helen Maldonado died during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male prison space; 2022 complaint over cruel/inhuman/degrading treatment of trans women in Lago Agrio; 2024 allegations of forced head-shaving, beatings and violence targeting breast/body implants; 2026 death in State custody of a 23-year-old trans woman drew calls for an independent investigation at the El Encuentro maximum-security prison. The program explicitly does NOT push a one-size placement rule, instead advocating individualised housing decisions per Inter-American standards considering gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, and cites the July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty.

prison_adds.title: Trans Women Report Being Punished for Their Identity in Ecuador Prisons (Spanish)
prison_adds.summary: Pulitzer Center investigation: Ecuador's prisons are 'almost always male' - the last prison census counted 73 trans women across all Ecuadorian prisons (organisation Fundacion Vivir Libre says there are many more), and trans women are placed in male pavilions. Case: Venezuelan trans woman Alexa (27) detained Aug 2023 at Penitenciaria del Litoral was initially sent to male pavilion 9 with three other trans women rather than the 'prioritaria' pavilion reserved for vulnerable populations (where many sexo-gender-diverse inmates are held); she received no medical exams or HIV treatment there. The story documents rapes and torture reported to be directed at prisoners' gender identity, showing placement practice operates by birth sex/legal sex with protective 'prioritaria' placement used unevenly.

records.current_summary:
South Atlantic island settlement with its own assembly: same-sex activity legal since 1989, equal age of consent since 2005, and full equality in April 2017 when the assembly approved same-sex marriage and civil partnerships 7-1, on a public consultation showing 90 per cent support for marriage and 94 per cent for partnerships — the registrar confirmed the law the following June, adoption followed the same year, the constitution bans sexual-orientation discrimination, and the first Pride was held in the capital that April. An official of the community described it as 'open, tolerant and respectful'; note that the much more remote dependencies administered from the same capital did not follow on marriage.

The earlier profile's inherited arithmetic and its borrowed UK custody stories have been deleted: on the surviving evidence the legal picture here is stronger, not weaker, than the administering state's, and there is no source indicating the GB single-sex-services code extends to the territory.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in the Falkland Islands (Wikipedia; Prisons Ordinance 2017 equal-treatment clause)
prison_adds.summary: Thin: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in the Falkland Islands' article documents no trans-prisoner housing data for the territory - no birth-sex vs identity placement policy, no special units, no solitary/segregation practice - but its hate-crime section notes that the Prisons Ordinance 2017 (legislation.gov.fk, in force 2019-07-17) requires prison staff to treat all prisoners equally without distinction to, among other categories, sexual orientation; a statutory equal-treatment clause covering prison staff, with no trans-specific placement or segregation detail.

records.current_summary:
A self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, Guernsey moved briskly through the 2010s: in 2011 it aligned blood-donation rules with the metropole, ending the HIV-era ban on gay and bisexual donors; in June 2015 the states rewrote the adoption law to open adoption to same-sex couples, removing a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples; and in December 2015 the states approved same-sex marriage 37-7, rejecting civil-partnership and secular-union alternatives as insufficient, with the law itself commencing from spring 2018.

That record covers sexual orientation squarely; the position on gender identity was asserted in the earlier profile without any cited source and has been deleted, so a transgender visitor should treat legal gender recognition and trans-specific protection as unestablished here — the more notable local quirk being that, on the documented chronology, civil partnership arrived later than in the neighbouring dependency that shares the island group's institutions.

prison_adds.title: Guernsey Prison - Wikipedia
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia article on Guernsey Prison (Les Nicolles), the island's only prison: opened 1989, 11 wings, capacity 139, operated by the States of Guernsey and accommodating male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages (population ~99 in November 2024). Contains no birth-sex-vs-identity housing rule, no trans special unit, and no solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners; verdict thin: no usable finding on the prison-housing axis.

records.current_summary:
Ghana is dangerous for trans visitors — and narrowly avoided becoming much worse. In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill: up to 3 years in prison for simply identifying as LGBT, and 5 years for “promotion.” President Akufo-Addo refused to assent pending legal challenges, the Supreme Court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when the 8th parliament dissolved — but its unanimous passage and broad public support signal the political climate, and reintroduction is expected.

Under existing law, “unnatural carnal knowledge” carries up to 3 years, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. Accra has a resilient underground community (LGBT+ Rights Ghana — whose 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks), but nothing that can protect a visitor.

prison_adds.title: Ghana parliament passes bill criminalising gay acts
prison_adds.summary: BBC (30 May 2026): Ghana's parliament approved a new bill criminalising homosexuality and the promotion of LGBTQ+ activities; it proposes that identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer be punished by up to three years' imprisonment, adds a 'duty to report' prohibited acts to police, and was passed under pressure from religious leaders on President Mahama, whose ratification is still required. Establishes the direct state pathway by which trans people in Ghana can be imprisoned for identity alone - the population to which any prison-placement practice would apply - while containing no provision on how such prisoners would be housed.

prison_adds.title: People 'panicking' as Ghana passes sweeping law criminalising LGBTQ+ activity
prison_adds.summary: The Guardian (1 Jun 2026): the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill, passed by Ghana's parliament on 29 May 2026 and expected to be signed by President Mahama, mandates prison sentences of three to 10 years - up to three years for identifying as LGBTQ+ and longer for promotion/advocacy. Community groups (e.g. One Love Sisters Ghana) report panic, eviction risk and self-censorship. The article contains no information on prison placement of trans prisoners, confirming the absence of any publicly documented housing policy for them in Ghana.

records.current_summary:
Greece is a workable destination with a clear law-versus-practice gap. The legal framework is among Europe's strongest — it ranks 7th on the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map, has banned conversion therapy and intersex infant surgery, has a hate-crime law covering gender identity, and legalised same-sex marriage in 2024 (the first Orthodox-majority country to do so). There are no trans-specific border or bathroom restrictions, and the government is progressive with an improving trajectory.

But the social reality lags the law. A mob of about 150 people assaulted two trans people in Thessaloniki; an European Court of Human Rights case documented police detention and mistreatment of trans sex workers; surveys show Greeks are markedly more avoidant of public LGBTI visibility than the EU average (63% avoid holding hands); and the UK Foreign Office has issued an LGBTQ travel warning for Greece.

Major tourist destinations — Mykonos, Athens's Gazi district, Thessaloniki — are welcoming; outside them the climate is rougher than the law suggests.

prison_adds.title: Φυλακές Κορυδαλλού: Τρανς κρατούμενες θα μεταχθούν για πρώτη φορά στη γυναικεία πτέρυγα (LiFO)
prison_adds.summary: LiFO (4 Dec 2021): four trans detainees were ordered transferred to the women's prisons of Korydallou (Athens) by decision of the General Secretary for Crime-Prevention Policy Sofia Nikolaou, after each had petitioned for transfer stating they identify and wish to be treated as women. The four (three Greek, one Bulgarian) had been held at Trikala and Corfu prisons, effectively isolated and treated inconsistently with their self-identified gender. First documented transfer of trans prisoners to a women's facility in Greece; it illustrates that default placement had followed the male facilities and that an on-request transfer route to women's facilities existed.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Greece — Correctional Facilities section (Wikipedia)
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia's overview of Greek LGBTQ rights records under 'Correctional Facilities' that since 4 December 2021 trans women detainees, upon their request, may be relocated to correctional facilities for women — the policy change matching the Korydallou transfers reported by LiFO the same day. Placement thus starts from the registered sex, with a 4 Dec 2021 decision creating an on-request transfer route for trans women; the article documents no special trans units and no rule covering trans men's placement.

records.current_summary: Grenada demands real caution. The buggery law (10 years) remains on the books (no successful court challenge yet), though unenforced; no LGR; small community; tourist areas insulated.

prison_adds.title: Grenada Stakeholder Report for the UN Universal Periodic Review: LGBTIQ+ Rights (The Advocates for Human Rights, Khaleem Ali, GrenCHAP)
prison_adds.summary: UN UPR stakeholder report (submitted 11 Oct 2024): because Grenada has no laws permitting legal gender change, 'the Government also prosecutes transgender women – who are considered legal men under the law.' The report provides no prison-specific housing/segregation detail, but it establishes the operative placement framework: a trans person's legal status, and so any correctional classification, follows registered/birth sex rather than gender identity. No special unit, solitary/segregation practice, or trans-prisoner housing case/ruling is documented for Grenada.

prison_adds.title: Grenada 2023 Human Rights Report (US State Dept)
prison_adds.summary: US State Dept 2023 report (pub. Feb 2024): Grenada's sole penitentiary, designed for about 200 persons, held 385 prisoners as of August 2023, including six women in a separate block; conditions were harsh due to gross overcrowding, with potable water in men's-block hallways but not cells. The report documents gendered blocks and general detention conditions but records no transgender-specific housing policy, special unit, or segregation practice, and no trans-prisoner cases or complaints.

records.current_summary:
Guatemala demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: Asociación Lambda's observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022 — hundreds of incidents and dozens of deaths — with 35 victims saying they intended to flee the country. Guatemalan officials have explicitly excluded trans women from femicide-law protection on the grounds they are not “biological women.” There is no legal gender recognition and no SOGI hate-crime statute (a 2022 law actually increased penalties for “aggravated” LGBT visibility before being struck down).

Congress has repeatedly advanced anti-LGBT initiatives (Law 5276, the 2022 “Life and Family Protection” bill, later shelved after protests). The community is organised (a local group such as Lambda, plus trans collectives) but under pressure. Tourist areas (Antigua, Atitlán) are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from the general violence level.

prison_adds.title: Every Day I Live in Fear: Violence and Discrimination Against LGBT People in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, and Obstacles to Asylum in the United States (Human Rights Watch)
prison_adds.summary: HRW (7 Oct 2020), Guatemala chapter: 'Guatemalan authorities facilitate anti-trans violence is by placing trans women in men's prisons, exposing them to violence, including sexual assault.' Bárbara Herrarte, trans activist with Redmmutrans (Red Multicultural de Mujeres Trans), described her time in a men's prison: 'Always, at night, someone got in my bed and forced me to have sex with him.' Documents birth-sex placement in the men's prison system as of 2020 with sexual-assault risk, and no gender-identity-based placement policy, special trans unit, or trans-specific solitary/segregation practice; LGBTQ org Lambda flags forced internal displacement from violence generally, but no trans-specific custody-policy or court ruling is documented in the report.

records.current_summary:
Honduras is dangerous for trans visitors. It is the site of the hemisphere's defining transfemicide case: Vicky Hernández, a trans woman and activist shot dead in 2009, whose case reached the regional Inter-American Court of Human Rights — which in 2021 found the Honduran state itself responsible for her death and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime. The ruling ordered reforms (including legal gender recognition, which Honduras has partially implemented), but violence against LGBT people remains at levels Amnesty called “epidemic,” driving mass asylum-seeking.

Nothing criminalises being trans, and the Vicky Hernández ruling created formal obligations; a name-change process exists. But gangs, security forces, and social actors all contribute to a documented pattern of violence against trans women in particular, and prosecution remains rare.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, but outing-violence probability is among the highest in the region, outside the two largest countries.

prison_adds.title: Penitenciarias Nacionales de Honduras: una tortura para personas LGTBI - Corresponsales Clave
prison_adds.summary: Corresponsales Clave (trans activist Kendra Jordany, 6 Sep 2017), drawing on the torture-prevention centre CPTRT: trans women in Honduras' national penitentiaries are held in the MEN'S system. At Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara, LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the 'La Isla' module (located beside the mentally-ill unit); trans women are forced to cut their hair and barred from presenting as women ('la policia... dicen que ellas son hombres'); conjugal visits are denied. At Penitenciaria de Marcala authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after CPTRT intervention was she isolated from the men and her feminine belongings returned. Documents birth-sex placement with de facto LGBTI grouping and ad-hoc protective isolation, and no placement-by-gender-identity policy.

prison_adds.title: HRW, 'Every Day I Live in Fear': Violence and Discrimination Against LGBT People in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, and Obstacles to Asylum in the United States
prison_adds.summary: Human Rights Watch (7 Oct 2020), Honduras section: 'Honduras places transgender women in men's prisons, which can lead to physical and sexual abuse.' A Honduran judge told HRW of a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards; the judge said she had informed prosecutors, who did not investigate: 'There's no way to protect trans women in men's prisons.' Independent confirmation that placement operates by birth sex in the men's system, with documented sexual violence and official inaction (as of 2020).

records.current_summary:
Haiti is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but the national government has effectively collapsed: gangs control most of the capital (Port-au-Prince), the police are outgunned, and mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition, no protection infrastructure, and no functioning judiciary.

The trans-specific risk is inseparable from the generalised collapse — outing in gang-controlled areas can be lethal. A 2018 official US State Department report described attitudes as hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity, particularly in the capital; freshness confirms trans people remain exposed to vagrancy-law fines with zero protection or hate-crime coverage.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Haiti - Wikipedia
prison_adds.summary: Thin for the prison-housing axis: the fetched article (HTTP 200) documents Haiti's legal framework - same-sex conduct legal since 1791, no legal gender-identity recognition, no anti-discrimination protections, and a June 2017 Senate bill penalising same-sex marriage with up to three years' imprisonment - plus documented harassment of transgender people in post-earthquake camps. It contains no prison-placement practice: no birth-sex-vs-identity housing rule, no trans special units, and no solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners; no usable placement finding.

records.current_summary:
Isle of Man: a self-legislating Crown Dependency in the Irish Sea whose parliament, Tynwald, works through its own bills on these questions. The House of Keys in 2005 proactively adopted a clause protecting employees from dismissal over sexual orientation, framing it in human-rights terms; the chief minister publicly committed to marriage equality in 2015, at a time when this parliament and Northern Ireland's assembly were the only British legislatures refusing it; the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill passed its final legislative stages in April 2016 and the first civil partnership was converted to marriage that July, preserving the couple's 2015 wedding date.

Current reference material confirms the settled picture: civil partnerships from 2011, marriage since 2016, and a legal gender-recognition right in force since 2009 alongside 'gender reassignment' protections in island equality law. Claims about the metropole's single-sex code and its statutory guidance were carried in the earlier profile without primary legislative support and have been deleted, leaving the local record as the basis of this entry.

prison_adds.title: Isle of Man Prison - Wikipedia
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia article on Isle of Man Prison (Jurby), the island's only functioning prison (GBP 41.7m facility at the former RAF Jurby, fully operational 14 August 2008), operated by the Isle of Man Prison Service. Documents separate units for remand and convicted prisoners, female prisoners, young offenders and vulnerable prisoners, plus a segregation unit - but no birth-sex-vs-identity placement rule, no trans special unit, and no trans-specific solitary/segregation practice; verdict thin: no usable finding on the prison-housing axis.

records.current_summary:
Ireland is a calm, comfortable destination for transgender visitors. It was one of the first countries to introduce legal gender recognition by self-declaration — the 2015 Gender Recognition Act lets adults change their legal gender without medical requirements — and bathroom use is unrestricted. A hate-crime law covering sexual orientation and gender identity took effect at the end of 2024, equality law bans discrimination in employment, housing and services, and marriage equality was approved by referendum in 2015.

The caveats are stagnation and a mildly worsening climate rather than active rollback. The 2015 law is binary-only and long-promised reform (non-binary, under-16s) has stalled; transphobic hate speech remains uncriminalised after a 2024 government U-turn; a university study in 2025 documented rising discrimination against sexual and gender minorities; and total hate-crime reports rose about 15% in 2025 (racism and xenophobia are the most common motives). None of this amounts to criminal exposure or physical danger for a visitor.

Day-to-day, the country is welcoming with low violent crime and a strong civil-society support network.

prison_adds.title: Guardian: Ireland's gender recognition act, a decade on (The Guardian)
prison_adds.summary: Guardian (23 Dec 2025) decade retrospective on the 2015 Gender Recognition Act: it documents the Barbie Kardashian case — a violent offender who changed name by deed poll and obtained a gender recognition certificate in 2020, then was transferred from a women's prison to a male prison during her sentence — as the case that made prison custody a focus of gender-critical campaigning in Ireland, and reports that an amendment to the GRA 'which would limit its scope so the certificate no longer changes sex for the purposes of imprisonment' has passed its first stage in the Oireachtas; the amendment was drafted by barrister Laoise de Brun (of The Countess), who cites UK gender-critical campaigners as inspiration.

prison_adds.title: Transgender history in Ireland (Wikipedia)
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia 'Transgender history in Ireland' (rev. 2 Oct 2026): documents Barbie Kardashian, a trans woman who held a Gender Recognition Certificate and a Department of Social Protection certificate recognising her as female — found guilty at Limerick Circuit Court in May 2022 of seven counts of threatening to kill or cause serious harm to her mother, and acquitted in October 2024 of separate alleged threats to a fellow prisoner and a prison officer at Limerick Prison; the article records that as of late 2025 a proposed amendment to the Gender Recognition Act 2015 that would limit the effect of a GRC 'for the purposes of imprisonment' had passed its first legislative stage, and cites the historical 1889 case of John Bradley (assigned female at birth), imprisoned at Grangegorman prison after disclosing.

records.current_summary:
Israel is the Middle East's most progressive destination for trans visitors, with no criminalisation, anti-discrimination protections, court-based legal gender recognition (with dead-name removal from IDs as of 2025), publicly funded transition healthcare, and Tel Aviv as a regional queer hub.

Two traveler-specific risks pull the score down. First, Ben-Gurion Airport has no regulations for interacting with trans travelers — documented humiliating questioning and detainment, with surgery demanded for gender recognition ("If you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male"). Every foreign visitor transits Ben-Gurion, making this a high-probability friction point. Second, violence is rising sharply: 433 homophobic/transphobic physical incidents were reported in 2025, including dating-app traps and organized ambushes, with transgender people "bearing the brunt." Trump's anti-trans rhetoric is reportedly inflaming the local climate.

The right-wing Netanyahu coalition and the Israel-Hamas war aftermath have weakened protections, though the National Security Committee has convened on LGBTQ public-space security.

prison_adds.title: Keepin’ It “Real”: Israel’s Segregation of Transgender Prisoners and the Transgender/Cisgender Binary (Lihi Yona, Buffalo Journal of Gender, Law & Social Policy, Vol. 24, p. 43)
prison_adds.summary: Law-journal article documenting that Israel’s response to transgender prisoners’ vulnerability has been to isolate/segragate them, keeping trans inmates apart from the rest of the prison population rather than placing them in facilities matching their gender identity. Establishes that a trans prisoner faces isolation-based custody as the default management practice.

prison_adds.title: New Israel Fund – Victory for Transgender Rights in Israeli Prisons
prison_adds.summary: October 2019 precedent-setting case: an Israeli court ordered the Israel Prison Service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and transfer her from a male prison to a female one, after ACRI petitioned. The prisoner was initially placed in a separate wing of the women’s prison, and ACRI prepared a further petition to have her housed with the general population — showing case-by-case placement review by the courts, and that trans women have at times been held in men’s prisons in Israel.

records.current_summary:
Jamaica is dangerous for trans visitors. The Offences Against the Person Act (buggery law, up to 10 years) remains on the books and shapes police culture; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The defining case is Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party after being outed — whose killing police failed to investigate, now the subject of an Inter-American Commission case (Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica) documenting state failure to protect trans life.

Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people remains a live risk — community members report that violence against trans people (beatings, stonings) is common but rarely reported because there is no point. Tourist resorts (Montego Bay, Negril, Ocho Rios) are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare, but a visibly trans visitor outside them faces real outing-violence risk with indifferent police.

prison_adds.title: Gays ostracised in prison – study
prison_adds.summary: Jamaica Gleaner reporting (5 Feb 2019) on UWI lecturer Carla Moore's 2018 study (Apr-Nov 2018, funded by the Inter-American Institute of Human Rights, the IBA and the UN Latin American Institute for the Prevention of Crime): Jamaicans perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender 'are isolated' in Jamaica's penal institutions and rehabilitation opportunities for them are 'basically non-existent'. Inmates' movement inside facilities is severely curtailed and access to resources often limited because of entrenched homophobia/transphobia - other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners. The study estimated that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at Tower Street Adult Correctional Centre belong to sexual or gender minorities and reported that lesbians face prevalent 'corrective rape'. Evidence that LGB/trans prisoners are socially ostracised and isolated rather than integrated, with no specialised housing policy documented.

prison_adds.title: Jamaica 2023 Human Rights Report (US Department of State)
prison_adds.summary: US State Dept country report: 'Prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity'; correctional facilities were significantly overcrowded (Tower Street maximum-security cells at three times capacity), with harsh, life-threatening conditions, and a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay. The report also records that Jamaica barred legal gender registration ('Individuals were not legally allowed to register a change of gender'), that the buggery law (up to 10 years' hard labour) criminalised consensual same-sex conduct, and that no anti-discrimination law protected SOGI. Official-state confirmation that trans prisoners face identity-targeted violence in Jamaican prisons with no gender-recognition framework for accommodation decisions.

records.current_summary:
Japan is a very safe destination for transgender visitors in practice, with a legal framework that lags behind. There is no national anti-discrimination law — the 2023 "understanding" law is symbolic — and legal gender change still requires a court process. But courts have moved in trans people's favour: the Supreme Court struck down the sterilisation requirement for legal gender change in 2023 and ruled workplace bathroom restrictions on a transgender woman illegal the same year.

Day-to-day risk is minimal: violent crime is rare, visibly trans visitors report curiosity more often than hostility, hotels and transport are unproblematic, and the capital and the second city have an established queer scene. The main practical challenge is the strictly gendered, full-nudity culture of hot springs (onsen) — manageable using guides to gender-neutral or private rental baths and mixed open-air baths, which travellers actively share.

Same-sex marriage remains unavailable, which matters for a trans visitor planning to travel with a partner on spousal status. One caveat: online transphobic rhetoric and misinformation rose visibly during the 2023 legislative debates, indicating a live culture-war current, though it rarely translates into street-level trouble for visitors.

prison_adds.title: Prison warned over treatment of transgender inmate | The Asahi Shimbun
prison_adds.summary: Asahi Shimbun (9 Sep 2023): Gifu's Kasamatsu Prison — a women's prison — holds an inmate who is listed as female on her family register but identifies as a man (diagnosed with gender identity disorder). The Gifu Prefecture Bar Association demanded the prison allow him male clothes and a male hairstyle; after years with no policy change, the bar association issued a formal 'warning' to the prison in Sep 2023. The case shows Japan places convicted trans inmates in facilities matching their registered (family-register) sex rather than their gender identity, while treatment conditions inside remain contested at the prefecture level.

prison_adds.title: Japan Should End Abusive Detention Conditions for Transgender People | Human Rights Watch
prison_adds.summary: HRW (11 Jun 2025): Tomoya Asanuma, a prominent transgender activist, was arrested in March 2024, held for more than 100 days in pre-trial detention and charged with assault; he was detained among men at a pre-trial detention centre, initially denied hormone treatment (until a doctor recommended it), mocked for his transgender identity in interrogations, and only allowed to shower away from other detained men after requests. HRW frames this as part of Japan's 'hostage justice' detention abuse and the legal limbo trans people face. For the prison-housing axis, it documents that a trans man's custodial placement followed his male legal sex, with accommodations (hormones, segregated showers) granted only grudgingly.

records.current_summary:
Kyrgyzstan is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct has been legal since 1998 and there is no expression statute, but legal gender recognition has been removed, police abuse and extortion of LGBT people are documented, and an active anti-LGBT political campaign is running in the country — in 2023-2024 two discriminatory laws targeted the LGBTI community and restricted LGBTI organisations, with homophobic and transphobic legislator rhetoric accompanying them.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but LGR removal, a police extortion culture, and the political campaign make being outed risky.

prison_adds.title: Kyrgyzstan: Events of 2024 — Human Rights Watch World Report 2025
prison_adds.summary: thin: no usable finding — the HRW World Report 2025 Kyrgyzstan chapter contains no content on transgender prisoners or prison housing; its only prison references concern journalists and opposition activists sentenced to prison terms (media repressions, freedom of expression), not placement or conditions of trans detainees.

records.current_summary:
Cambodia is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — the country has never criminalised same-sex activity or gender expression — and the government is formally cooperative: it accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations at its 2024 Universal Periodic Review, including legal gender recognition, and hosted the UN Independent Expert on SOGI in 2023. Phnom Penh and Siem Reap, the country's two main cities, have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors.

The risks are street-level and police-level rather than legal: a human-rights organisation documents "shocking" harassment and abuse of transgender women in urban centres, including a reported police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse). There is no legal gender recognition yet, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute.

For a visitor: low probability of legal trouble; moderate probability of harassment if visibly trans outside tourist areas; police are a risk factor, not a protection, for trans women especially.

prison_adds.title: CHRC says transgender rights are observed in prison
prison_adds.summary: Khmer Times (19 Feb 2025) reports Cambodian Human Rights Committee (CHRC) president Keo Remy, speaking at the handover of an ambulance to Correctional Centre 2 at Prey Sar prison in Phnom Penh, said Cambodia observes transgender prisoners' rights: transgender offenders who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from Correctional Centre 1 (the men's facility) to Correctional Centre 2 (the women's facility). The statement was made in praise of the centre, not as a published regulation, and no statute or formal policy text is cited; the article also flags that prison overcrowding has worsened because of gang-crackdown arrests. This is the only direct documentation of trans-prisoner placement practice for Cambodia found in two search rounds.

records.current_summary: South Korea is broadly workable for trans visitors — there is no criminalisation, courts have protected trans people's restroom access and ruled favourably on legal gender recognition, and Seoul hosts one of Asia's largest Pride parades. There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner, and no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering services. No severe incidents involving trans visitors are documented. Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are welcoming; outside them, more caution is warranted.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in South Korea (Wikipedia)
prison_adds.summary: One Wikipedia full-text search round surfaced no dedicated article on trans prisoners in South Korea; the jurisdiction's LGBTQ-rights article documents its only prominent trans-in-state-placement case, military rather than civilian: Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, a transgender conscript, was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical/mental handicap; she died by suicide in March 2021; the Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021; and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty. The same article records that consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel is criminalised under Military Criminal Act article 92-6 (up to two years' imprisonment; a gay soldier was sentenced to six months in 2017) and that transgender people are excluded from military service. It contains no information on how transgender prisoners are housed in South Korea's civilian prison system - no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, special unit, or solitary/segregation practice is described. (Last-resort encyclopedic source; fetched and verified.)

records.current_summary:
Sri Lanka is dangerous for trans visitors. Sections 365/365A of the 1883 Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women), and Human Dignity Trust lists Sri Lanka as criminalising the gender expression of trans people: police use vagrancy and “cheating by personation” provisions against trans people. The International Commission of Jurists identifies Sri Lanka Police as “the foremost perpetrators of human rights violations against LGBTI individuals” — harassment, arbitrary detention, and abuse are documented as systematic, though formal prosecutions remain limited.

There is no legal gender recognition (a 2016 recognition circular exists but is not law), no anti-discrimination protection, and no hate-crime statute. Colombo has a small organised community (EQUAL GROUND) and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners, which moderates but does not remove risk: the realistic worst case is police harassment or detention under personation/vagrancy provisions rather than prosecution.

prison_adds.title: Future prison constructions: Transgender inmates to receive separate accommodation
prison_adds.summary: Sri Lanka's Prisons Department has no dedicated transgender housing today: Media Spokesperson/Commissioner Gamini Dissanayake (Oct 2024) said current prison facilities make giving transgender prisoners their own space impossible, and separate accommodation is only planned for prisons built in the future. Placement is decided case-by-case: trans detainees holding the recognised identity card (issued since the June 2016 gender-recognition-certificate circular) are accommodated per their preferred gender 'where possible', while those without it go through a doctor's assessment of whether they 'can be considered a transgender' before placement, weighing inmate preference. Officials explicitly worry about people accused of sex offences 'identifying as transgender' to enter female housing with born-male offenders, a stated reason for resisting gender-based placement. Outcome: placement by birth sex is the practical default in the current male/female ward system, with a medicalised, discretionary exception process and no statutory placement rule.

prison_adds.title: Future prison constructions: Transgender inmates to receive separate accommodation
prison_adds.summary: The Morning (original Daily Morning reporting, 4 Oct 2024) of the same Prisons Department statement: Commissioner Dissanayake said 'we always try to accommodate transgender prisoners who have the official identity card', and absent the ID a doctor assesses whether the inmate can be considered transgender, after which 'the preference of the particular inmate' feeds the accommodation decision. The piece also reports the Committee for Protecting Rights of Prisoners (CPRP) asking that future prisons give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space (including possible space within prison hospitals), citing that 'developed countries have recognised transgender rights'. Confirms the absence of a codified placement policy and the official preference-assessment route as of Oct 2024.

records.current_summary:
Luxembourg is exceptionally safe — among the strongest trans jurisdictions in its region. Legal gender recognition by self-determination has existed since 2018 (Act of 10 August 2018) with no medical requirements, and notably the process is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is banned across employment, goods, services, education, and health; a national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018; an equality body handles complaints.

No traveler-facing concerns exist: no bathroom laws, no border issues (entry under the common border-free travel zone), no documented anti-trans violence pattern. Gaps are minor: no nonbinary marker, and gender expression and sex characteristics are not explicitly covered in anti-discrimination law — a visitor-specific impact is not documented.

prison_adds.title: Prisons luxembourgeoises : Les détenus gays et transgenres sont protégés
prison_adds.summary: L'essentiel (26 August 2015), reporting Justice Minister Félix Braz's parliamentary answer to LSAP MP Cécile Hemmen, documents that Luxembourg prisons place inmates who disclose or openly show LGBT/trans identity so they are sheltered from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners, with trans-detainee situations handled case by case (the administration gathers all available information on the prisoner); such cases are described as 'exceptional'. Requests by LGBT detainees to be placed in an ordinary section are generally granted, and the minister warned against solutions that would stigmatise or isolate these detainees. A 1989 grand-ducal regulation requires staff to address detainees by surname, and penitentiary staff honour a detainee's chosen 'Monsieur'/'Madame' form of address. The Justice Ministry kept no statistics on LGBT prisoners (disclosure cannot be compelled without illegal privacy interference), and the planned Uerschterhaff prison (Sanem) was designed with multiple sections so detainees could be separated by sex, personality, grounds of detention and, among these, sexual orientation. Outcome: placement follows disclosed identity/need on a case-by-case basis with no codified birth-sex rule and no documented special custody unit or solitary/administrative-segregation practice for trans prisoners in Luxembourg.

records.current_summary:
Moldova is workable for trans visitors — the best-protected in its immediate neighbourhood. Since 2022, anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes are criminal offences covering SOGI explicitly, and the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover sexual orientation and gender identity; the capital Chisinau's Pride marches through the city centre under police protection, and police have deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters seeking to disrupt it.

Counterweights for a visitor: no accessible legal gender recognition exists for anyone (a medicalised process exists on paper but is reported not functional in practice); the predominant Orthodox Church and major politicians (including the capital's mayor) regularly issue homophobic statements that colour the climate; and the breakaway separatist region of Transnistria, controlled by the neighbouring power Russia, has its own anti-LGBT "propaganda" law — travelers should treat that region as a separate, much riskier jurisdiction.

prison_adds.title: Trăind de gardă/ Deținut transgender – dublu condamnat în închisoare de către „oamenii cu epoleți”
prison_adds.summary: Moldovan investigative outlet Ziarul de Gardă (15 June 2024) documents the four-year detention of Igor Brumarețchi, a transgender man (registered female at birth in 1972, documents changed to male in 2007), who served his sentence in Moldova's penitentiary system, mostly at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca. He says he was held alone in unsanitary, rat-infested cells — including for long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit ('izolator disciplinar') — supposedly for his own safety, while his request for sector 12 (the unit for detainees requiring protection) was refused. He describes staff humiliation: forced strip body searches, 'go to the gynaecologist' calls over the intercom, opening his bathroom door, and calling him 'Natașa' at roll-call, and says only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The National Penitentiary Administration (ANP) replied that he was detained alone 'at his own written request' and without any rights being violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed; Brumarețchi says he will sue in Moldovan courts and the ECtHR, and ZdG has notified the Ombudsman and GENDERDOC-M. Outcome: de facto placement of a trans detainee by birth sex in the men's system with prolonged solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, and no special-unit option.

prison_adds.title: Deținuți ai prejudecăților în instituțiile de stat. Persoane LGBT+, la un pas de suicid. Povestea tragică a unui locuitor al satului Dubna
prison_adds.summary: Observatorul de Nord (7 April 2025) corroborates the same case: Igor Brumarețchi from Dubna village (Soroca district) spent three years locked alone in a cell at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, fully isolated from other detainees and humiliated by prison staff on grounds of sexual orientation, which brought him to the edge of suicide. The piece states the authorities admit homophobia still persists in state institutions and say they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment; the full investigation appeared on anticoruptie.md. Confirms the solitary-style isolation placement practice for a trans detainee in Moldovan prison No. 6 as of 2025.

records.current_summary:
Mexico pairs meaningful legal progress with one of the world's highest tolls of violence against transgender people. Twenty-two of its 32 states offer administrative legal gender recognition, Mexico City and Nayarit have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections exist.

Against that, 71 trans or gender-diverse people were murdered in a single recent year — the second-highest figure in the Americas after Brazil — with organised crime increasingly involved and impunity near-total. The victims are overwhelmingly local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit, not tourists; violence is also highly concentrated by region.

In major tourist destinations and central Mexico City, heavily policed and progressively governed, a trans visitor's everyday risk is closer to harassment than violence. The dominant hazard for any traveller is Mexico's general crime environment. Use the Admin Divisions view: state-level scores range from among Latin America's best (Mexico City) to levels comparable with its most dangerous regions.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ people in prison (Wikipedia; Mexico section)
prison_adds.summary: Thin: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ people in prison' article, Mexico section, records only one Mexico-specific policy: in July 2007, through the efforts of the National Human Rights Commission (CDHDF), the Mexico City prison system began allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, with visitors not required to be married to the inmate, applying to all Mexico City prisons. The article contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement (birth-sex vs identity placement), special units, or solitary/segregation practice for Mexico.

records.current_summary:
Mali is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. In October-November 2024 the Transitional National Council adopted a new penal code criminalising homosexuality for the first time — with the Justice Minister declaring that anyone “engaging in, promoting or apologising for” same-sex relations will be prosecuted; vague drafting suggests broad application, and prior “public indecency” provisions (Art 225) were already used against gender-nonconforming people. The junta context means no independent judiciary, no civil society space, and active conflict in much of the country.

For a visitor: a brand-new criminalisation statute under a junta with no recourse, plus conflict conditions.

prison_adds.title: World Report 2025: Mali — Human Rights Watch
prison_adds.summary: Thin: no usable prison-housing finding. The HRW World Report 2025 Mali chapter (Events of 2024) covers the junta's rule, counterterrorism sweeps (arbitrary arrest of 25 people in Ouro Fero village, Nara region) and an ICC arrest warrant, but contains no transgender-specific content and no information on prison placement, special units, or solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners.

records.current_summary:
Malta is among the safest countries in the world for transgender visitors. It has ranked first for LGBTI legal rights in its region every year since 2015: gender identity and expression are protected from discrimination in law, legal gender recognition works by self-determination, and 'X' gender markers are available on passports. Conversion therapy is banned and the constitution guarantees LGBTI equality.

Malta records one of the lowest rates of physical or sexual victimisation of LGBTIQ+ people in its region, and the national police force has adopted hate-crime procedures for sexual-orientation and gender-identity incidents. A foreign government's diplomatic guidance describes the country as a safe environment for foreign LGBT travellers, and no government travel advisory flags trans-specific concerns.

Residual risks are minor: non-physical harassment (including online) is more common than violence and tends to be under-reported, and — in the unlikely event of arrest — prison practice has been found to lag the country's progressive law.

prison_adds.title: Seven transgender prison inmates awarded €5,000 each in damages for 'truly disgusting' treatment (Malta Today)
prison_adds.summary: Malta Today (29 May 2018): the Maltese civil court (Judge Silvio Meli) awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison €5,000 each (€4,000 for breach of rights plus €1,000 for damage to personal dignity) after the prison authorities held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, were forced to use the men's showers (often forgoing washing) and suffered insults and 'continuous sexual abuse and violence'. The court found the authorities had 'knowingly and repeatedly' placed them in situations of high risk of sexual and psychological violence; the only alternative offered, transfer to the female section, would have cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, and female inmates and warders were said to be hostile, so they stayed in the male section. The director of prisons was ordered to pay; the Aditus Foundation human-rights NGO represented the seven women.

prison_adds.title: The lived experiences of transgender inmates at Malta's Correctional Service Agency (Oriana Vidal, University of Malta, 2024)
