prison_adds.summary: University of Malta master's dissertation (Oriana Vidal, 2024) interviewing four current and former transgender/gender-diverse inmates of Malta's Correctional Service Agency (CSA), a cohort spanning the last 25 years. It records that after Malta's 2013 gender-law reform CSA practice allowed TGD inmates to transfer to the female section, whereas earlier practice had segregated them in a separate dormitory (staff described the rationale as 'the risks of pregnancies'); participants now receive individual cells in the female section but report residual misgendering by officers (masculine birth names), gender-appropriate clothing and healthcare gaps, and conclude that CSA practice, policies and procedures lag Malta's progressive national gender-identity law. It also cites the 2018 newspaper report (Agius, Malta Today) of seven TGD inmates winning a court award after rights breaches including strip searches, showering-privacy issues and being treated as males.

records.current_summary:
Mozambique demands real caution from trans visitors — one of Africa's better legal positions. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised under the 2015 Penal Code; courts ruled in 2017 that LGBTIQ organisations can register (Lambda Mozambique); and there is no documented pattern of police targeting. Counterweights: no legal gender recognition, no SOGI hate-crime statute, social hostility outside Maputo is significant, and the Cabo Delgado insurgency affects the north (a general, not trans-specific, risk).

For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest infrastructure; avoid the north.

prison_adds.title: Outright International: Mozambique country page
prison_adds.summary: Thin: no usable prison-housing finding. Outright's Mozambique overview (updated March 2026) covers decriminalised same-sex conduct (2015 penal code), absence of any legal gender-recognition procedure, and social barriers for LGBTIQ people, but contains no information on where transgender prisoners are housed, no placement rule, and no documented custody case involving a trans person.

prison_adds.title: Mozambique: Events of 2023 (HRW World Report 2024)
prison_adds.summary: Thin: no usable prison-housing finding. The HRW World Report 2024 Mozambique chapter (published 11 Jan 2024) documents general police detentions and election-related arrests but contains no transgender-specific content and no prison-placement information for trans prisoners.

records.current_summary:
Nigeria is among the most severe environments for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the SSMPA (14 years, applies to all including tourists), and 12 northern states apply Sharia law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct. A transgender TikToker known as "Abuja Area Mama" was found beaten and dead on a highway in Abuja; police misgendered her in death and, six months later, no one has been arrested. Police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for "looking gay" — the SSMPA has been described as a "weaponised" law — and dating-app "kito" gangs use Grindr to lure victims into assault and robbery. The UK Foreign Office has warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks.

A proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public. Trans identity is NOT explicitly criminalized nationally (the SSMPA targets same-sex conduct), and the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists. But the Sharia death penalty, the trans-specific killing with impunity, the police brutality, and the UK advisory make this an environment to avoid entirely.

prison_adds.title: Bobrisky — Wikipedia (Nigerian transgender woman; 2024 imprisonment at Kirikiri)
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia biography of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, documents the only trans-imprisonment case the search surfaced: she pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine. She served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, and was released on 5 August 2024. At sentencing, press coverage (BBC Pidgin, cited in the article) openly asked 'which prison they will keep the crossdresser in', reflecting discretionary placement; the article does not record whether she was assigned to a male or female section. Outcome/ruling: an October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

records.current_summary:
The Netherlands is a very safe destination for transgender visitors: official WorldPride 2026 guidance confirms visas and entry depend only on nationality, not gender identity, passports with amended or "X" gender markers are accepted, and no medical documentation is needed at the border. Discrimination based on gender identity is prohibited by law, and since July 2025 a discriminatory motive is a statutory aggravating factor that can increase penalties by up to a third.

Practical safety supports are strong: Amsterdam operates dedicated reporting networks for LGBTQIA+ incidents, the mayor and police committed to priority investigation of Pride-period incidents for 2026, and the capital is among Europe's safer cities for ordinary crime. Same-sex marriage is legal and non-binary people are recognised, so a trans traveller's partner status raises no border or legal problems.

The genuine caution is rising reported hostility: discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people reached 4,800 last year, up 51% in a year for transgender-specific reports and 81% since 2022, and many queer residents avoid public displays of affection. For a visitor this chiefly means a risk of harassment or verbal abuse, particularly late at night, rather than systematic danger.

prison_adds.title: NJCM adviseert demissionair Minister voor Rechtsbescherming over plaatsing van transgender gedetineerden (Nederlands Juristen Comité voor de Mensenrechten)
prison_adds.summary: The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights (NJCM), criminal-law working group, announced (site date 22 Feb 2024) that it had advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection on the placement of transgender detainees: no law or regulation currently governs their placement, which NJCM calls worrying and undesirable. The note highlights the group's vulnerable position (international research documents human-rights violations including discrimination and sexual violence), the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands, and the relevance of CPT standards, pointing to the full letter (PDF) to Minister Weerwind (21 Feb 2024).

prison_adds.title: Advies plaatsing transgender gedetineerden — brief aan de Minister voor Rechtsbescherming (NJCM Werkgroep Strafrecht, 21 februari 2024)
prison_adds.summary: NJCM letter to Minister Weerwind (Leiden, 21 Feb 2024) documenting Dutch placement practice for transgender detainees: there is no law, regulation or official policy governing their placement — the Penitentiary Principles Act only separates male and female detainees — and DJI (Prison Service) confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in the BRP (municipal records) together with case-by-case factors (gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, physical/mental health), while DIZ said it was (unpublished) drafting guidelines. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'Extra Care Facility' (EZV) wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. The letter cites documented cases: a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing at arrival then moved to an EZV; a parole-board appeals ruling (21 Mar 2016, 15/4323/GB) on a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation in the men's prison; and sentencing rulings by the Limburg court (17 Oct 2017, ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624, trans woman facing placement in a men's prison) and The Hague appeals court (29 Jun 2020, ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108, trans man in a women's prison) treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM asks the minister to create CPT-aligned rules placing transgender detainees by gender identity.

records.current_summary: Nauru demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2016; tiny population (~12,000); no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence; the asylum-detention legacy shaped its international image but not its LGBT law. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Nauru (Wikipedia) — Nauru Regional Processing Centre Rules 2014 gender-identity non-discrimination clause
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia's LGBTQ rights in Nauru article documents the only detention-related gender-identity provision found for Nauru: the Nauru Regional Processing Centre (RPC) Rules 2014, made under the Asylum Seekers (Regional Processing Centre) Act 2012, ban discrimination against any person based on sex or gender, sexual preference or gender identity within the RPC immigration-detention facility. This covers immigration detention, not Nauru's criminal-justice prison system, and concerns non-discrimination rather than placement by birth sex vs identity, special units, or solitary-confinement practice. No documented data was found on where transgender prisoners are housed in Nauru's corrections system, nor any trans-prisoner case or ruling.

records.current_summary:
New Zealand is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Legal gender recognition by self-declaration has been in force since 2023 (Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act); the Law Commission reviewed Human Rights Act protections for trans, non-binary and intersex people in 2024; and takatāpui/rainbow communities have deep institutional recognition. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction.

The counterweights are documented and significant for the street climate: reports of gender-identity hate crimes jumped 42% between 2022 and 2023 (161 to 229 incidents), spiking around the Posie Parker visit (the visiting campaigner); the national survey (Counting Ourselves) found almost 1 in 5 trans and non-binary people were threatened with physical violence in four years, and 8% experienced it; and community advocates accuse police of failing rainbow communities amid far-right agitation (library events crashed, church arson threats).

For a visitor: full legal protection; moderate probability of harassment in charged spaces; functioning (if criticised) institutions.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ people in prison (Wikipedia; New Zealand section)
prison_adds.summary: New Zealand: citing Dalzell, Pang & Broemdal 2024 (Australian & New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry, 'Gender affirmation and mental health in prison'), the article reports that trans people in New Zealand prisons are more likely to have prior experience of abuse and show a higher rate of incarceration, and that the NZ government has declared support for gender-affirming healthcare and gender-affirming clothing for incarcerated persons. No placement rule (birth-sex vs identity housing), special unit, or solitary/segregation practice for New Zealand is described.

records.current_summary:
Oman is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — it combines an explicit anti-trans statute with a documented trans-traveller abuse case. The 2018 Penal Code criminalises "imitating the opposite sex" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, a provision that extends to foreign nationals. Enforcement is documented: in January 2018 the national police force announced arrests of transgender women after private-party photos circulated on social media; an international human-rights organisation documented further arrests and convictions under the provision.

Most concretely for travellers: in February 2024 a foreign non-binary traveller arriving at the capital's airport on a tourist visa was pulled aside while friends cleared immigration, taken to a private room, forced to remove their shirt, touched inappropriately, and denied entry to the country. They warned publicly: "if you identify as someone from the community, do not go to these countries."

Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the same code, so partner travel carries the same exposure; consensual same-sex activity risks prosecution for foreign nationals too.

prison_adds.title: Playing dress-up: Four cross-dressers jailed in Oman — Roya News
prison_adds.summary: Roya News (19 Sep 2018), on the Public Prosecution's announcement: a Salalah preliminary court sentenced two men to four years in jail and fined them OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and sharing photos of themselves in women's clothes on social media, and two further men to three years with the same fine for featuring in the video; the sentences fall under the July 2018 Omani Penal Code provision (Article 22), under which 'any male that appears in female clothing or demeanor' may be fined up to OMR 3,000 and jailed up to one year, with additional 'publishing immoral acts on social media' charges. The article notes these follow January 2018 arrests by the Royal Oman Police of a group of men for dressing as women after social-media photos circulated. It documents court-ordered imprisonment of gender-nonconforming people in Oman, but contains no information on where inside the prison system those convicted were housed.

records.current_summary:
The Philippines is one of the most socially accepting destinations in the region for trans visitors, with deep cultural traditions of gender diversity, a vibrant Pride scene in the capital, and no criminalisation — trans identity has never been criminalised in this country.

However, there is a "near-complete absence of legal protections at the national level": no national legal gender recognition law at all (so identity documents cannot be corrected and retain the birth gender), the SOGIE Equality Bill — a national anti-discrimination law — has been stalled for 25 years, and there is no marriage equality. Documented violence includes the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman found in a river (June 2025), a foreign national arrested for raping a trans woman at a resort (May 2025), and a drag artist assaulted mid-performance. The national human-rights commission actively investigates discrimination cases but lacks enforcement power without a national law.

For a visitor: no border friction and genuinely warm social acceptance, but the legal-protection vacuum means limited recourse if discriminated against at a venue — documented incidents include bathroom, fitting-room, and resort denials; partner or marriage-based protections do not exist.

prison_adds.title: Inside jails, gay men and trans women ‘wed’ fellow PDLs to escape abuse (Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism, by Aie Balagtas See)
prison_adds.summary: Investigative feature on Manila City Jail: transgender women and gay men are held in the ordinary MALE dormitories (mandatory head-shaving on arrival for the male dorm), where they assume housekeeping/entertainer roles and informal same-sex “weddings” with male inmates are widely used by gangs as a survival/protection strategy against abuse. Documents that trans women in Philippine jails are housed by birth sex in male facilities with no gender-matched placement, and that safety comes from inmate hierarchies rather than policy.

prison_adds.title: BJMP-Davao transfers LGBT inmates to annex facility for safety (SunStar Davao, by Ian Carl Espinosa)
prison_adds.summary: Official practice documented: BJMP-Davao Community Relations chief Jail Senior Inspector Ellen Rose Saragena said LGBT detainees at Davao City Jail are relocated in batches to the City Jail Annex “to prevent abuse”, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens; three LGBT groupings live in the annex since its establishment. Shows the official Philippine response is administrative segregation of LGBT detainees into a separate annex for “safety”.

records.current_summary:
A US territory: the federal anti-trans turn of 2025–26 (document/marker rules, TSA screening friction) applies in full — and unlike some territories, local law compounds rather than softens it. In July 2025 Puerto Rico's governor signed the most severe ban on gender-affirming care in the United States, criminalising provision of hormones or surgery to anyone under 21 even with parental consent — up to 15 years' imprisonment, $50,000 fines, loss of medical licences, with parents potentially exposed; civil-rights groups announced court challenges, and the signatory had campaigned presenting as LGBTQ-friendly.

Local politics have swung both ways: the island's marriage ban was dismantled in the federal courts after local couples sued (2014), while religious-freedom and conversion-therapy bills advanced in 2019 before the governor withdrew them under organised pressure. For a trans visitor today: federal paperwork friction, the country's harshest local care-crime regime, and a visible advocacy community pushing back in court.

prison_adds.title: Executive Order 14168 ("Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government") - Wikipedia
prison_adds.summary: Executive Order 14168 (signed 20 January 2025) directs US federal agencies, including the Bureau of Prisons, to recognize only two sexes, and federal practice has followed by placing transgender inmates in facilities congruent with their sex assigned at birth rather than their asserted gender identity. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order violates the Prison Rape Elimination Act's requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided on an individual safety assessment. Federal custody rules apply in Puerto Rico as a US territory; the search found no separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit, or ruling.

records.current_summary:
Rwanda demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, and the government formally tolerates a small LGBT presence — but a 2025 Human Rights First Rwanda Association submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents ongoing law-enforcement abuses against transgender persons, including arbitrary arrests and detentions (framed as “vagrancy” or “deviance” round-ups in Kigali's periodic street-cleaning operations).

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but Kigali's sweep operations can net gender-nonconforming people, and recourse is nil. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and the constitution recognises only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman — a partner-travel consideration for a trans visitor.

prison_adds.title: Rwanda's transgender community face violent detentions for being trans (VICE World News)
prison_adds.summary: VICE World News (20 Nov 2020): although being transgender is not criminalised in Rwanda, police routinely arrest trans women on pretext charges — 'homelessness', drug sales, theft — and detain them at Kigali's Gikondo Transit Center, a facility for people exhibiting 'deviant acts or behaviors'. Bella was held there after police falsely claimed she was homeless and sold drugs; as punishment she was confined in a tiny dark cell known as 'the cat box' and raped by fellow detainees at least three times. Gabi was detained at Gikondo for six months in 2018; Nunu was detained there three times between 2018 and 2019. Detainees are supposed to be charged within 72 hours or transferred to a police station, court, rehabilitation facility, or jail, but trans detainees are held for indeterminate periods in facilities lacking transparency. Documents placement practice: trans prisoners are held under a 'deviance rehabilitation' framework in transit centres (with segregated/confining cells used as punishment), not in facilities matching their gender identity.

prison_adds.title: Outright International: Rwanda country page
prison_adds.summary: Thin-to-useful: Outright's Rwanda page (updated March 2026, based on a July 2025 Human Rights First Rwanda Association submission to the UN Human Rights Committee) reports transgender individuals face heightened risks of harassment at identity checks and arbitrary arrests on grounds such as 'vagrancy' or 'public order' offenses, and that LGBTIQ people flee arbitrary arrests, detention and ill-treatment. It corroborates the detention pattern for trans people but gives no prison-placement (men's vs women's facility) detail.

records.current_summary:
El Salvador demands real caution from trans visitors — in an unusual transition. Historically it was among the world's most dangerous places for trans women (documented life expectancy of 35 years, among the lowest anywhere; the Camila Díaz Córdova case — a trans woman deported from the US and killed — became the first hate-crime homicide prosecution of its kind). Since 2022, President Bukele's gang crackdown collapsed the national homicide rate by ~98% (107 to 1.9 per 100k), dramatically reducing the gang violence that drove much anti-trans predation.

The trade-off is a state of exception (an exceptional security regime) with mass arbitrary detention (tens of thousands imprisoned, over 75,000 reported, minimal due process) — a risk mechanism that falls on anyone police decide to target, including gender-nonconforming people, with no effective recourse. There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative name change only), no SOGI hate-crime statute, and no institutional protection infrastructure.

prison_adds.title: Jennifer, la mujer trans que sobrevivio a las torturas en las carceles del regimen de excepcion (GatoEncerrado)
prison_adds.summary: GatoEncerrado (Oscar Hernandez, 26 Feb 2024): since the state of exception began (Mar 2022), trans women arbitrarily captured in mass raids are held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. Jennifer, arrested 14 Apr 2022 in San Salvador, was held first at the 'El Penalito' police lockups and then in prison, where custodians forcibly shaved her hair ('para que sepan lo que son'), singled her out with another trans woman (Rosa) for outdoor punishment drills (handcuffed, forced squatting in the sun), and denied her HIV clinic access; a judge freed her after ~4 months finding the arrest unsupported, while Rosa remains imprisoned. Organisations (Socorro Juridico Humanista, Cristosal) link the abuse to the absence of a Gender Identity Law. Documents birth-sex placement in the general prison system with trans-targeted abuse and no special custody provision.

records.current_summary:
Thailand is one of Asia's most accepting destinations for transgender visitors. Visible gender variance is part of mainstream culture (the kathoey tradition long predates modern categories), the state actively promotes LGBTQ tourism, same-sex marriage became legal in January 2025 as the first in Southeast Asia, and the Immigration Bureau runs a dedicated "Welcome Pride" initiative to smooth entry for travellers whose passports don't match their appearance or gender. Gender-affirming healthcare is a mature, accessible industry.

The gaps are legal rather than social: there is still no procedure to change one's legal gender marker, the 2015 Gender Equality Act is weakly enforced, and — as the 2025 murder of a Thai trans woman in Pattaya highlighted — Thailand has no hate-crime law, so bias-motivated violence is prosecuted as ordinary crime.

For a visitor the practical risks are mostly Thailand's general ones: nightlife disputes, scams, and alcohol-fuelled incidents, with some reported friction in resort nightlife districts. Everyday movement, hotels, healthcare, and transit are unproblematic.

prison_adds.title: Thailand Separates LGBTQ Inmates, Considers Segregated Prison (NBC News/AP)
prison_adds.summary: NBC News/AP (29 Jan 2017): the Thai Department of Corrections says LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993; at Pattaya Remand Prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men. Trans woman Theerayut Charoenpakdee, stopped by police and expecting to be 'thrown in prison with all the men because I still have the title of Mr.,' was instead held in the separated wing. The government was also discussing what could be the world's first exclusively-LGBTQ prison facility (the Min Buri pilot), while accepting that transgender women elsewhere usually face a choice of men's cells or solitary. Of roughly 300,000 Thai prisoners, more than 6,000 were registered as sexual minorities.

prison_adds.title: Exclusion or protection? Activists skeptical about LGBT prison (Coconuts Bangkok)
prison_adds.summary: Coconuts Bangkok (30 Aug 2016): trans activist Nachacha Kongudom, arrested in June 2015 while protesting the junta, was sent to a men's prison against her request for a women's facility; prison officials told her that under Thai law 'she remains a man' and no Thai document can identify a trans woman as female, and during intake she was harassed and ordered to expose her body. The Department of Corrections then announced a pilot using Bangkok's Min Buri prison as an LGBT facility to prevent abuse of trans inmates, after Pattaya men's prison had already begun separating trans prisoners from cis men following reports of abuse. DOC figures: ~4,448 of ~300,000 prisoners identified as LGBT, 34 of them transgender. Activists welcomed the pilot but feared it 'could encourage exclusion' and insisted placement 'should be an option, not an obligation.'

records.current_summary:
Tajikistan is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but police conducted a series of raids against LGBTIQ people in several cities in 2022-2023, and documentation in the country shows systematic patterns: discrimination in all spheres, police abuse, arbitrary detention, and forced disclosure. There is no transparent legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and authorities have previously maintained informal registries of LGBT citizens.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but police raids, registry practices, and zero recourse make discovery dangerous.

prison_adds.title: Tajikistan: Events of 2024 — Human Rights Watch World Report 2025
prison_adds.summary: thin: no usable finding — the HRW World Report 2025 Tajikistan chapter contains no content on transgender prisoners or prison housing; its prison/detention references concern opposition figures (Group 24, Islamic Revival Party detainees) and deportees, not placement or conditions of trans detainees.

records.current_summary:
Trinidad and Tobago demands real caution from trans visitors — legally improved, socially dangerous. The courts struck down the colonial buggery laws (Jones v. AG, 2018, upheld on appeal), removing criminalisation of same-sex intimacy; but there is no legal gender recognition, no SOGI anti-discrimination protection, and parliament has repeatedly rejected reforms (the ruling party's constitution review again refused SOGI protections in 2024).

Documented street risk is substantial: community advocates report trans people are still “beaten, stoned and chopped,” with most incidents never reported; and police have publicly warned of a spate of Grindr ambush robberies — criminals using fake profiles to lure LGBT victims to meetings followed by armed robbery (multiple cases through 2023-2024, including a Cocorite man beaten and robbed). This dating-app predation pattern is a direct traveler concern.

prison_adds.title: Protect transgender inmates'
prison_adds.summary: Trinidad Express (Camille Hunte, 28 Nov 2018) on the official 'Justice through a Gender Lens' Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers (launched Nov 2018 by the CCJ, CAJO, UN Women, JURIST Project, TTAWJ and the Judicial Institute of TT): the Protocol states plainly that 'in Trinidad and Tobago, there are no special facilities in our penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities'. It directs judicial officers sentencing a person whose gender identity does not accord with their birth certificate to use recommendations to prison authorities to ensure provisions are in place for the inmate's physical safety, and instructs courts to refer to intersex/transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and permit court access irrespective of dress. Official acknowledgment that housing placement for trans prisoners is discretionary, unsafe, and mediated only through sentencing recommendations - with no facility of its own.

records.current_summary: Turkey presents real, structured danger for trans visitors — institutionalised, presidential-level hostility that has become state policy. Police profile and detain trans women for identity checks (20 detained in Istanbul in July 2025), trans women have historically been frequent targets of torture and ill-treatment by police, and a trans woman attacked with a knife was herself detained (victim-criminalised). Transphobic attacks and Pride-event violence are documented, and foreign visitors must carry original passports at all times — creating outing risk at the frequent transit checkpoints. A draft law leaked in October 2025 would criminalise LGBT people — not yet passed but under active government consideration. The risk is concentrated in urban trans-visible contexts (Istanbul's Beyoğlu/Tarlabaşı) rather than package-holiday tourist zones, but the institutional hostility pervades.

prison_adds.title: Rights groups urge probe into 'suspicious' death of transgender prisoner in Turkey (Stockholm Center for Freedom)
prison_adds.summary: SCF (18 Dec 2025): transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and Turkish rights groups (coordinated from Human Rights Association / IHD branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakir, Mersin and Aydin) demanded an independent investigation and changes to 'detention practices affecting transgender prisoners'. Kaos GL-cited accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers say four transgender inmates were collectively sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators only entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; opposition MP Sevda Karaca (EMEP) raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025. The case documents that Turkey holds trans prisoners in gendered facilities by registered sex (a trans man was held in a women's prison) and that trans-prisoner custody conditions were formally contested at the state level in late 2025.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQI+ prisoners are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches (Kaos GL), reporting the Prison Insider 'Country Profile' on Turkey (with CİSST data)
prison_adds.summary: Kaos GL (7 May 2024), covering the Prison Insider Country Profile report on Turkey prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association (CISST) and using ILGA World data: LGBTI+ prisoners in Turkish prisons are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches and to de facto isolation, being placed in solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and sometimes refusing to go to hospital out of fear of other male prisoners during transfers. CISST observations quoted in the article state that there is no policy or staff training to identify and address LGBTI+ prisoners' needs, that Turkish prison administration is built on a binary, heteronormative system, that LGBTI+ prisoners are frequently transferred (disrupting visits and solidarity), and that complaints are ineffective and can lead to further violence. The piece documents that Turkey manages trans and LGBTI+ prisoners through segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement.

records.current_summary:
Uruguay is one of Latin America's safest and most progressive destinations for trans visitors. The Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law 19,684, 2018) provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration (no surgery or diagnosis required), a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a state employment quota for trans people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 (Latin America's first), and bathroom access is legally protected.

The country is consistently ranked among Latin America's safest (Global Peace Index), with a "strong democratic governance structure and positive record of upholding political rights and civil liberties" (Freedom House). However, a 29-year-old trans woman, Joana, was shot dead in her home in Montevideo in July 2025 (the assailant was sentenced to 7 years), and discrimination incidents have been documented at a hospital (San Carlos) and a bank (BROU). Freedom House notes "disparities in treatment" for transgender people despite legal equality.

For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms protected, no criminalisation, and Montevideo is welcoming.

prison_adds.title: Uruguay to build prison for transgender inmates — MercoPress
prison_adds.summary: MercoPress (29 Jul 2023), citing Uruguayan authorities and officials: as part of a new prison planned for Montevideo there will be a specific sector for the trans population, which Parliamentary Commissioner for the prison system Juan Miguel Petit called 'good news for a very vulnerable population' and estimated would be ready in less than two years. National Rehabilitation Institute (INR) Director Luis Mendoza told a parliamentary hearing that 'if the trans person enters the system they have the right to decide if they want to go to a men's or women's prison,' and that while trans women are currently placed in female prisons, cohabitation entails 'a whole process' of adaptation; he also noted the new women's prison at Punta de Rieles would for the first time account for the trans population, adding 'the laws are very advanced in Uruguay, but the mentality and infrastructure are not in line.' The article cites official figures of 14,965 people deprived of liberty, including 28 trans women and nine trans men (Office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Prison System).

records.current_summary:
Vatican City is workable for trans visitors — an unusual case: a tiny 0.49 km² tourist enclave with essentially no resident jurisdiction a traveler can fall afoul of. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; there are no bathroom inspections, no morality police, and the guards and gendarmerie do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of tourists of every presentation visit annually without incident; entry is via the neighbouring city of Rome with no border formality.

The doctrinal climate is hostile — the 2024 declaration "Infinite Dignity" condemned gender-affirming surgery and "gender theory" as violations of human dignity, and no legal recognition or protection of any kind exists — but this is a climate signal, not a traveler-facing mechanism: the realistic worst case for a visitor is being refused entry to the basilica over a dress-code dispute (shoulders/knees rules apply to everyone).

prison_adds.title: Crime in Vatican City
prison_adds.summary: Vatican City operates no prison system: the article states there are only a few cells used for pre-trial detention, and persons sentenced to imprisonment by Vatican City serve their time in Italian prisons, with costs covered by Vatican City. Because no domestic prison system exists, there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, trans custody facility, or documented trans-prisoner placement case for this jurisdiction. (Last-resort encyclopedic source; no separate State Department Holy See chapter for 2023/2024 exists.)

records.current_summary:
Vietnam is broadly workable — described as one of the most tolerant countries in the region toward sexual minorities. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the 2015 Civil Code (Article 37) was a landmark recognising transgender people's right to change their legal gender. However, the implementing Gender Affirmation Law has been stalled for over eight years — the right exists on paper but not in practice. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity.

No trans-specific killing has been documented here. Conversion efforts (SOGICE) are documented, and healthcare discrimination is a significant barrier — trans people face stigma and "red tape" in accessing care, and trans-competent providers are scarce.

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, unrestricted bathroom access, and no criminalisation — but the stalled recognition means no practical gender-marker change on documents. This country is under one-party authoritarian rule, where an international human-rights organisation finds that "rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice"; a UN development agency is actively engaged on trans-rights strategies.

prison_adds.title: Social News 16/1 — Separate jails proposed for transgender, gay prisoners
prison_adds.summary: VietnamNet (16 Jan 2015) reports a proposal by the Social, Economic and Environmental Institute to Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security to house homosexual and transgender prisoners in jails separate from the general prison population, to protect them from sexual harassment; the institute cited US California statistics that 67% of homosexual and transgender prisoners had suffered sexual harassment and a 2014 survey finding that most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails. Critically for the placement lane, the institute stated that under Vietnam's then-current prison infrastructure transgender prisoners could only be held in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population — i.e. no housing wing matched to the prisoner's gender identity existed — and asked that prisoners be allowed to determine their own gender identity. No enacted outcome or newer documented placement practice was found in the two search rounds conducted.
